chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
title: Fletcher Henderson's difficult keys and brother Horace
summary: Crawford says Henderson wrote in unusual keys that challenged players such as Roy Eldridge, and mentions Horace Henderson in Colorado.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: What kind of material was the band playing when you were --
Well, we were playing stocks all the time.
No, I mean Fletcher Henderson's band.

Oh, see, Smack Henderson, who was the leader, he wrote for his band, put it in every kind of key other than C or B flat. That was the hardest band, as Roy Eldridge said, that he ever played with, because he had -- the band had the men playing in all those different keys, see, and he wasn't used to that. He was used to playing with bands like Zack White, Helvey and all those type of bands, (inaudible) arrangements.
What were they playing mostly, in B flat, C and F?
No, no, no, I mean the other bands.
Yeah, something like that. That's the most, if that -- any more than two keys. Fletcher, he'd write some mean stuff. I may have asked you this. Did you know his brother Horace?
I just know of him. I've never met him.

Very much of a gentleman, nice fellow. He's living in Colorado Springs. He lived in Denver, but he's been working seven nights a week in Colorado Springs. He's got a ten acre farm out in Denver, he and his wife, cows, even goats, raising some chickens, and he enjoys it. He's a country boy now.
But he came here to play a big -- they gave a tribute to him. So we attended one night.
That was last year. Right. Right.
And so he went back to Colorado.
